opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was a tough one, and honestly I still think about it sometimes.

Beam search was one of those features that looked very reasonable on paper. It came from the machine translation era, people had used it for years, and when we started building the inference engine it felt natural to support it. But as the system grew, we realized it was quietly costing us a lot.

The core problem is that beam search doesn't fit the way a modern high-throughput inference engine works. Most of our design assumes each request is a sequence, or a few independent samples, that we can schedule, batch, and manage memory for very efficiently. Beam search breaks that. Beams fork and get pruned at every step, they share prefixes, and you have to keep comparing scores across them. That logic spread into the scheduler, the memory manager, and the sampler. Every time we wanted to optimize something, or add something like better prefix caching or a new scheduling policy, we had to ask, "Does this still work with beam search?" Often the answer was no, or it required a lot of special-case code.

So the question became: who is this complexity for? When we looked at actual usage, it was a fairly small group. Most people using large language models today use sampling, or greedy decoding, or they generate several samples and rerank. For chat models in particular, beam search often doesn't even give better results; it tends toward bland, repetitive output. Meanwhile, the cost was paid by everyone, because it slowed development of the core engine and made it harder to keep things correct and fast.

The users who objected were not wrong. Some had real workloads that depended on it, like certain translation or structured-output tasks, and from their perspective we were taking something away. I understand that frustration. In open source, when you remove a feature, the people who rely on it are very loud, which is fair, while the people who benefit from a simpler, faster system mostly don't notice. They just get a better engine and never connect it to that decision.

What we tried to do was not just delete it and walk away. We gave people a path: you can implement beam search on top of the engine, outside the core, using the primitives we expose, like generating multiple candidates and getting log-probabilities. It might be a bit slower for those specific cases, but it keeps the core clean. To me that's the right division: the engine should do a small number of things extremely well, and more specialized algorithms can live as a layer above.

The bigger lesson for me is that maintaining a widely used project is largely about saying no. Adding features is easy and makes people happy right away. Removing them is painful, but if you never do it, the system collapses under its own weight and you can't keep up with how fast the field is moving. In this area hardware changes, model architectures change, and usage patterns change every few months. If the codebase isn't flexible, you lose. So I'd make the same decision again, though maybe I'd communicate earlier and more clearly why we were doing it.

r001.rationale: The response says beam search no longer fits a modern high-throughput inference engine and conflicts with the engine’s primary scheduling, batching, and memory-management approach.

r002.rationale: It explains that beam search spreads special-case logic through the scheduler, memory manager, and sampler, making optimizations and new scheduling policies harder to adapt and maintain.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was one of the harder calls we made in vLLM, and I want to be careful about how I describe it, because I don't think the users who objected were wrong.

The context is this: vLLM started as a research project around PagedAttention, and the whole design of the engine assumes a certain kind of request. One prompt comes in, it gets scheduled, it generates tokens, each sequence is more or less independent. Beam search breaks that assumption. You have a group of candidate sequences that have to be expanded and pruned together at every step, and the number of live sequences changes constantly. To support that properly, the scheduler, the block manager, and the sampler all had to carry special-case logic. Every time we wanted to change something fundamental, like speculative decoding, chunked prefill, or prefix caching, somebody would ask, "but what happens with beam search?" And the answer was usually that it either didn't work or we had to spend a week making it work for a feature that a tiny fraction of users actually relied on.

So the question we asked ourselves was: what is vLLM for? Our judgment was that it's a serving engine for production workloads, and the overwhelming majority of those workloads are sampling or greedy decoding for chat and generation. Beam search is very important in some domains, translation, some structured outputs, certain research settings. But it was costing us velocity on the things that mattered to the majority.

Where I'll admit we could have done better is on the communication side. We moved it out of the core engine and reimplemented it at a higher level, essentially as a client-side loop over the regular generate API. Functionally it still exists. But it's slower, and for people who had built pipelines on the old behavior, that felt like a regression, and they told us so loudly on GitHub. I think if I did it again I'd spend more time explaining the tradeoff up front rather than letting people discover it in a release note.

The broader lesson I took from it is that an open source project cannot say yes to everything. If you try, the codebase becomes something nobody can maintain, and in the end every user suffers. Saying no to a vocal minority in order to serve a quiet majority is uncomfortable, but I think that's part of the job of a maintainer. You just have to be honest about what you're trading away.

r001.rationale: The response says beam search breaks the engine’s request assumptions and repeatedly complicates changes to core features such as speculative decoding, chunked prefill, and prefix caching, while identifying sampling and greedy decoding as the primary workloads.

r002.rationale: The response describes special-case logic and added effort to adapt engine features around beam search, but does not say that support would make adaptation between models and the inference engine increasingly complex.

astra-6.text:
I think users’ objections deserve to be taken seriously, because they’re telling us that something they rely on is going away. But supporting a feature also has a cost, and in an inference engine that cost can affect the complexity and maintainability of the whole system.

For me, the question is whether beam search needs to be part of the core engine, and whether its value justifies that ongoing cost. Removing it is a tradeoff, not a claim that nobody should use it.

I would judge the decision by how well we understood the affected use cases and how clearly we communicated a path forward. And if users show us important cases that we haven’t accounted for, we should be willing to revisit it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses beam search’s costs and whether it belongs in the core engine, but does not say it no longer fits evolving algorithms in the primary large-model inference workflow.

r002.rationale: It mentions complexity and maintainability in general, but does not explain that ongoing beam search support makes adaptation between models and the inference engine increasingly complex.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the objections deserve to be taken seriously. If someone depends on beam search, removing it creates a real cost for them. At the same time, maintaining a feature in an inference engine has a cost too, and that can affect how quickly the engine improves.

For me, the question is whether that tradeoff is justified. I’d want to understand the workloads that need beam search, whether alternatives actually meet those needs, and what a reasonable migration path looks like. If we haven’t answered those questions clearly, we owe users a better explanation—and we should be willing to revisit the decision if the evidence points the other way.

r001.rationale: The response discusses feature maintenance and engine improvement, but does not say beam search no longer fits the evolving algorithms in the primary large-model inference workflow.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain that supporting beam search would make adaptation between models and the inference engine increasingly complex.
